SQP Working-Set Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Working-set transfer from an SQP quadratic subproblem to the nonlinear iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constraints \(h(x)=0\) and \(g(x)\leq0\), form at \(x_k\) the SQP subproblem \[\min_p\ \nabla f(x_k)^{\mathsf T}p+\tfrac12p^{\mathsf T}B_kp\quad\text{subject to}\quad h(x_k)+J_h(x_k)p=0,\quad g(x_k)+J_g(x_k)p\leq0.\] Solve it by an active-set QP method, obtaining \(p_k\), multipliers, and terminal working set \(W_k^{\mathrm{QP}}\). A merit-function or trust-region globalization selects the accepted step, \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\). Initialize the next working set from constraints in \(W_k^{\mathrm{QP}}\), retaining constraints with compatible multiplier signs and adding newly blocking nonlinear constraints. Stop when primal feasibility and the Lagrangian-gradient residual are below tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SQP iteration obtains its direction and candidate active set from a linearized-constraint QP, then globalizes the step and transfers the accepted working set.
assumptions_latex: \(B_k\) is symmetric and makes the QP locally well posed.
The QP solver returns a primal-dual working-set solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((p_k,W_k^{\mathrm{QP}})\) supplies both the nonlinear trial step and the next active-set estimate.

The SQP working-set interface forms \[\min_p\

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SQP working-set interface constructs a quadratic model of the Lagrangian and linearizes every constraint. An active-set QP solver selects the constraints active at the subproblem solution. This QP working set is the SQP method's estimate of the nonlinear problem's optimal active set. The subproblem solution supplies the primal search direction and its multipliers supply a new multiplier estimate. A line search, trust region, or filter may modify acceptance of the step without changing the definition of the local QP working set.

With the exact Lagrangian Hessian and a correctly identified active set, the local iteration is a Newton iteration for the reduced KKT system.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Globalization Breaks Blind QP Working-Set Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes activity at an SQP subproblem solution from activity at a shortened nonlinear step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an SQP subproblem be formed at \(x_k\), and suppose an inequality \(g_i(x_k)+\nabla g_i(x_k)^\top p_k\le0\) is active at its solution \(p_k\). If globalization accepts \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\) with \(0<\alpha_k<1\), then QP activity alone does not imply \(g_i(x_{k+1})=0\), even for affine \(g_i\). For example, with \(g(x)=x\le0\), \(x_k=-1\), \(p_k=1\), and \(\alpha_k=1/2\), the QP endpoint is active but \(g(x_{k+1})=-1/2<0\). Therefore a transferred working set must be reconciled with the accepted point or deliberately treated only as a warm start.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint active at the full QP step can be inactive after a shortened SQP step, so the QP working set cannot automatically be declared active at the accepted nonlinear iterate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence contract for an active-set iteration
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let an active-set method generate states \(\sigma_k=(x_k,\lambda_k,\mathcal W_k)\) for a constrained problem with solution set \(X^*\) and optimal active-set map \(\mathcal A(\cdot)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract finite-dimensional convergence interface separating global approach, finite termination, and post-identification local rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An active-set convergence interface is a tuple \[\mathfrak C=(\mathcal G,\mathcal I,\mathcal R,\mathcal T),\] where \(\mathcal G\) is a globalization predicate implying that every relevant accumulation point is stationary, \(\mathcal I\) is the identification predicate \(\exists K\ \forall k\geq K:\mathcal W_k=\mathcal A(x^*)\), \(\mathcal R\) specifies the local rate after identification, and \(\mathcal T\) is the finite-termination predicate \(\exists K:x_K\in X^*\) with termination at \(K\). Each component must state its own hypotheses; no component is implied merely by naming the interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An active-set convergence interface records four logically distinct claims about a generated state sequence: a globalization claim for remote starting points, an eventual active-set identification claim, a local convergence-rate claim once the correct set is fixed, and an optional finite-termination claim. The interface is satisfied only for the components whose hypotheses and conclusions have been explicitly established. In particular, convergence to a stationary point does not by itself imply finite identification, and identification does not by itself imply superlinear convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interface exposes the separately quantified predicates \(\mathcal G\), \(\mathcal I\), \(\mathcal R\), and \(\mathcal T\) on the sequence \(\{\sigma_k\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Identification can be written as eventual constancy of the working set at the target active set.
Finite termination can be written as existence of a finite first hitting time for the certified solution set.
special_cases_latex: A convex-QP active-set method may satisfy \(\mathcal T\) without requiring an asymptotic rate.
A globalized SQP method may satisfy \(\mathcal G\), \(\mathcal I\), and a quadratic local-rate predicate.
immediate_consequences_latex: Failure of strict complementarity may invalidate \(\mathcal I\) while leaving a weaker stationarity conclusion possible.
boundary_notes: This is an abstract packaging of convergence properties, not a convergence theorem.
No inspected source states this four-component object as a canonical definition.

notation.meaning: Globalization, identification, rate, and termination predicates.

review_flags: The supplied sources state the component properties separately but do not define this unified convergence interface.
A source explicitly supporting this packaging is required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of finite-state termination reasoning without nonrecurrence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal W=\{W^a,W^b\}\) and define \(T(W^a)=W^b\), \(T(W^b)=W^a\). Then \(W_{k+1}=T(W_k)\) uses only two states but never terminates. Hence finiteness of the working-set family alone does not imply finite termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A process may alternate forever between two working sets.
assumptions_latex: No progress invariant or anti-cycling rule is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\mathcal W|<\infty\not\Rightarrow\text{ finite termination}.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-State Cycling Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional finite termination of an exact convex-QP working-set method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a feasible active-set method for a strictly convex quadratic program with finitely many inequalities. Assume each working-set subproblem is solved exactly, each nonterminal transition either makes strict primal objective progress or performs a zero-displacement pivot, and an anti-cycling rule prevents recurrence of the complete finite working-set state associated with an exact subproblem solution. Then only finitely many transitions occur. If the method stops exactly when the current point is primal feasible, stationary, and has sign-feasible working-set multipliers, it terminates at the unique global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact strictly convex QP active-set method terminates finitely when a valid anti-cycling rule excludes recurrence of its finite combinatorial states.
assumptions_latex: The QP is feasible and has \(H\succ0\).
There are finitely many inequalities and exact working-set solves.
The anti-cycling rule excludes recurrence of complete degenerate states.
The stopping test is the convex-QP KKT test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The method terminates after finitely many transitions at the unique KKT minimizer.}
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-State Noncycling Termination Interface
Finite-Termination Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite termination of a noncycling primal active-set method on a strictly convex QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a feasible primal active-set method for a quadratic program with finitely many linear inequalities and a strictly convex objective. Suppose every nonzero step strictly decreases the objective, every equality-constrained working-set subproblem is solved exactly, and a deterministic anti-cycling rule prevents repetition during degenerate zero-length pivots. In exact arithmetic, only finitely many distinct working sets can be visited without repetition. Consequently the method terminates after finitely many additions and deletions at a feasible point \(x_*\) whose working-set multipliers have the required signs. The primal feasibility, stationarity, and multiplier-sign conditions are the KKT conditions, so \(x_*\) is the unique global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A noncycling exact active-set method for a strictly convex QP visits only finitely many working sets and terminates at the unique KKT minimizer.
assumptions_latex: The QP objective has \(H\succ0\) and the linear feasible set is nonempty.
Nonzero steps strictly decrease the objective.
Degenerate pivots obey an anti-cycling rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method terminates finitely at the unique minimizer \(x_*\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite termination of a certified active-set method
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let an active-set algorithm generate \((x_k,\mathcal W_k)\) and let \(C\) be its terminal certificate set, such as the KKT set of a convex quadratic program.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-arithmetic finite termination; the principal specialized case is a primal active-set method for a strictly convex QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The algorithm has the finite-termination property on a problem class \(\mathcal P\) if \[\forall P\in\mathcal P\ \forall\sigma_0\in\operatorname{Dom}(P)\ \exists K<\infty:\ \sigma_K\in C(P)\quad\text{and the algorithm stops at }K.\] For the strictly convex-QP active-set interface, \(C(P)\) is the QP KKT set, and the standard finite-termination regime additionally requires that every nonzero computed search direction be followed by a strictly positive step, thereby excluding a zero-movement working-set cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite termination means that every admissible run in the stated problem class reaches a state carrying the required terminal certificate after finitely many iterations and stops there. It is stronger than asymptotic convergence. For the standard primal active-set method on a strictly convex quadratic program, the terminal certificate is primal feasibility together with stationarity and admissible multiplier signs. The usual finite-termination statement assumes that a nonzero computed direction always produces a positive step; this rules out cycling in which the iterate remains fixed while working sets are repeatedly added and deleted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists K<\infty\) such that \(\sigma_K\in C(P)\) and no state \(\sigma_{K+1}\) is generated.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The terminal hitting time \(\tau_C=\inf\{k:\sigma_k\in C(P)\}\) is finite for every admissible initial state.
special_cases_latex: For a strictly convex QP, the KKT point is the unique global minimizer.
If a finite-state working-set method never revisits a certified working-set minimizer and encounters such a minimizer periodically, termination is finite.
immediate_consequences_latex: Finite termination implies eventual identification only when the terminal certificate uniquely determines the optimal active set.
boundary_notes: Floating-point tolerance termination is not the exact finite-termination property.
Degenerate zero steps can permit cycling unless an anti-cycling assumption or rule is imposed.

knowledge_statements.title: Post-Identification Fast-Convergence Phase
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local quadratic SQP convergence after finite identification of the strongly active constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_*\) be a KKT point of a twice continuously differentiable nonlinear program. Assume LICQ, strict complementarity, and the strong second-order sufficient condition hold at \(x_*\). If an SQP sequence converges to \(x_*\), uses the exact Lagrangian Hessian, and identifies the active inequality set after some index \(K\), then for \(k\geq K\) its subproblem is locally the equality-constrained Newton system on the identified active manifold. Once unit steps are accepted, the primal-dual iterates \(z_k=(x_k,\lambda_k)\) satisfy \(\|z_{k+1}-z_*\|\leq C\|z_k-z_*\|^2\) for all sufficiently large \(k\) and some \(C>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under standard nondegeneracy and second-order assumptions, exact-Hessian SQP becomes equality-constrained Newton after active-set identification and converges quadratically with unit steps.
assumptions_latex: LICQ, strict complementarity, and strong second-order sufficiency hold at \(x_*\).
The SQP sequence converges to \(x_*\) and finitely identifies its active inequalities.
Exact Lagrangian Hessians and eventually accepted unit steps are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|z_{k+1}-z_*\|\leq C\|z_k-z_*\|^2\) for all sufficiently large \(k\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fast local phase after active-set identification
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((x_k,\lambda_k,\mathcal W_k)\to(x^*,\lambda^*,\mathcal A(x^*))\) be an active-set SQP sequence, and let \(e_k=\|(x_k,\lambda_k)-(x^*,\lambda^*)\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local smooth SQP near a KKT solution after the QP working set has settled at the nonlinear optimal active set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A post-identification fast-convergence phase begins at an index \(K\) when \[\mathcal W_k=\mathcal A(x^*)\quad\forall k\geq K,\] so the inequality-constrained iteration reduces locally to the equality-constrained iteration on the identified active manifold. It is quadratic when \(e_{k+1}\leq Ce_k^2\) for all sufficiently large \(k\), and Q-superlinear when \(e_{k+1}/e_k\to0\). Exact-Hessian local SQP has the quadratic form under the standard smoothness, LICQ, and second-order sufficient conditions; suitable quasi-Newton Hessians yield the superlinear form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The post-identification phase is the tail of an active-set iteration after the working set equals the target active set and no longer changes. The active inequalities can then be treated as equalities, so the local SQP step has the structure of an equality-constrained Newton or quasi-Newton step. Fast convergence means that the resulting primal-dual error is quadratic for an exact Lagrangian Hessian or superlinear for a qualifying quasi-Newton approximation. Identification and fast rate are separate requirements: the rate statement begins only after eventual working-set equality has been established.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After \(\mathcal W_k=\mathcal A(x^*)\) eventually, exact-Hessian SQP is locally quadratic and a qualifying quasi-Newton SQP is locally superlinear under their respective hypotheses.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The phase is an equality-constrained SQP iteration on the manifold defined by the identified active constraints.
Q-superlinear convergence is \(\lim_{k\to\infty}e_{k+1}/e_k=0\).
special_cases_latex: Under LICQ, strict complementarity, and second-order sufficiency, the local QP active set agrees with \(\mathcal A(x^*)\) for sufficiently close primal-dual iterates.
With exact second derivatives satisfying the stated local assumptions, the primal-dual pairs converge quadratically.
immediate_consequences_latex: Once identification holds, no further active-set combinatorial changes are needed in the local model.
boundary_notes: Strict complementarity is used for the stated active-set identification result and is not automatic.
Globalization safeguards must eventually permit the local step if the fast rate is to be observed.

notation.meaning: First index after which the target active set remains identified.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Method-neutral interface between working-set trials and standard globalization mechanisms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), a working-set model proposes a trial step \(p_k\) and predicted progress. A globalization mechanism accepts, rejects, shortens, or regularizes that trial using a merit-function line search, trust-region ratio, filter test, or restoration phase. The primal iterate and persistent working set are updated from an accepted trial; a rejected trial instead changes the step length, radius, model, penalty, filter, or restoration state. Global convergence and finite-acceptance conclusions require the assumptions of the selected mechanism and do not follow from the working-set model alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A globalization layer tests working-set trials before committing the primal point and persistent activity state; its guarantees depend on the chosen line-search, trust-region, filter, or restoration mechanism.
assumptions_latex: A working-set model supplies a trial step and a predicted-progress quantity.
One specified globalization mechanism supplies its own acceptance test and safeguards.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Persistent iterate and working-set updates are committed only through the selected acceptance contract.}
knowledge_statements.title: Accepted-Trial Globalization Contract
Globalization Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Merit-function globalization of a working-set or SQP search direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible or restoration-corrected iterate \(x_k\), compute a working-set direction \(p_k\) and choose an exact-penalty merit function \(\Phi_{\rho_k}\). Increase \(\rho_k\) until the predicted directional derivative satisfies \(D\Phi_{\rho_k}(x_k;p_k)<0\). Starting with \(\alpha=1\), reduce \(\alpha\leftarrow\beta\alpha\), where \(\beta\in(0,1)\), until \(\Phi_{\rho_k}(x_k+\alpha p_k)\leq\Phi_{\rho_k}(x_k)+\sigma\alpha D\Phi_{\rho_k}(x_k;p_k)\), where \(\sigma\in(0,1)\). Set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha p_k\), update the working set using accepted-point activity and multiplier signs, and stop when feasibility and KKT residuals are below tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Globalize each working-set direction with an exact-penalty Armijo line search, then update activity only from the accepted point and its multiplier information.
assumptions_latex: The selected merit function is directionally differentiable along \(p_k\).
The penalty parameter can be chosen so that \(p_k\) is a merit descent direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted step satisfies the Armijo decrease inequality for \(\Phi_{\rho_k}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Merit-based globalization of an active-set SQP step
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(p_k\) be an SQP or active-set model step at \(x_k\). Let \(\Phi(x;\mu)\) be a scalar merit function combining objective and constraint violation, and let \(D\Phi(x_k;\mu;p_k)\) be its directional model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Line-search globalization for smooth finite-dimensional constrained optimization; trust-region and filter mechanisms are nearby alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A merit-function globalization interface chooses \(\mu_k\) so that \(p_k\) is a descent direction for \(\Phi(\cdot;\mu_k)\), then selects \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\) satisfying \[\Phi(x_k+\alpha_kp_k;\mu_k)\leq\Phi(x_k;\mu_k)+\eta\alpha_kD\Phi(x_k;\mu_k;p_k),\qquad 0<\eta<1,\] and sets \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\). The interface accepts the full local step when \(\alpha_k=1\) satisfies the test and otherwise reduces the step until the prescribed progress condition holds or invokes a declared restoration or failure branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A globalization interface mediates between a locally motivated active-set or SQP step and acceptance from a remote starting point. In the merit-function form, constraint violation and objective value are combined into a scalar function. The penalty parameter is chosen so that the model step predicts descent, and backtracking selects a step length satisfying sufficient decrease. A full step is retained whenever it already passes the test. Trust-region or filter interfaces can play the same structural role but use different acceptance objects.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An accepted update satisfies the stated sufficient-decrease inequality and \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: A trust-region interface accepts according to agreement between actual and predicted reduction and updates a radius \(\Delta_k\).
A filter interface accepts using a partial order on objective and constraint violation rather than a single merit function.
special_cases_latex: For an exact \(\ell_1\) merit function, \(\Phi(x;\mu)=f(x)+\mu\sum_i|c_i(x)|\) in an equality-constrained problem.
Near a regular solution, a second-order correction may permit acceptance of the full SQP step.
immediate_consequences_latex: The accepted step need not solve the local model exactly.
A globalization mechanism can preserve a fast local phase only if it eventually stops shortening acceptable local steps.
boundary_notes: Globalization ordinarily guarantees stationarity or KKT accumulation only under additional boundedness, regularity, and subproblem assumptions.
The definition does not claim convergence to a global minimizer.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Taxonomy of failure boundaries for constrained NLP conclusions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For a constrained NLP instance \(P\), candidate solution \((x,\lambda)\), and algorithmic state \(\sigma\), let \(\mathfrak H\) denote the hypotheses required by a stated optimality, stability, identification, or convergence result.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An umbrella classification of mathematical and numerical events that invalidate hypotheses or conclusions in smooth finite-dimensional constrained optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A constrained-NLP failure-boundary taxonomy is a labeled decomposition \[\mathfrak F=\mathfrak F_{\mathrm{reg}}\cup\mathfrak F_{\mathrm{dual}}\cup\mathfrak F_{\mathrm{curv}}\cup\mathfrak F_{\mathrm{id}}\cup\mathfrak F_{\mathrm{comb}}\cup\mathfrak F_{\mathrm{num}},\] where the components respectively record failure of constraint regularity, multiplier or complementarity regularity, required curvature, active-set identification stability, finite working-set progress, and numerical reliability. An instance belongs to a component precisely when the corresponding explicitly declared hypothesis or certificate fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The failure-boundary taxonomy classifies why an optimality, sensitivity, identification, or active-set convergence statement may cease to apply. Regularity failures concern the relationship between active gradients and local feasible geometry. Dual failures include abnormal or nonunique multipliers and loss of strict complementarity. Curvature failures concern the reduced Hessian or critical cone. Identification failures concern unstable classification of active constraints. Combinatorial failures include cycling or repeated working-set misclassification. Numerical failures include rank loss, ill conditioning, and tolerance-dependent sign errors. Membership records a failed hypothesis; it does not imply that the optimization problem has no solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathfrak F\) is the union of the six declared failure classes, and overlaps are permitted.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The taxonomy may be represented by the set-valued label map \(L(P,x,\lambda,\sigma)=\{j:(P,x,\lambda,\sigma)\in\mathfrak F_j\}\).
special_cases_latex: A rank-deficient active Jacobian belongs to \(\mathfrak F_{\mathrm{reg}}\) and may also belong to \(\mathfrak F_{\mathrm{num}}\).
A weakly active constraint may belong to both \(\mathfrak F_{\mathrm{dual}}\) and \(\mathfrak F_{\mathrm{id}}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The classes are not mutually exclusive.
Failure of a sufficient hypothesis does not establish failure of the desired conclusion.
boundary_notes: This is a diagnostic classification, not a theorem asserting that all algorithms fail on every labeled instance.
No inspected source presents this exact six-class consolidated taxonomy.

notation.meaning: Failure class associated with one boundary mechanism.

review_flags: The blueprint requests a consolidated taxonomy, but the inspected books discuss the component pathologies in separate sections.
A source supporting the exact partition and terminology is required.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(x\) be feasible for \(c_i(x)=0\), \(i\in\mathcal E\), and \(c_i(x)\geq0\), \(i\in\mathcal I\). Let \(\mathcal A_I(x)=\{i\in\mathcal I:c_i(x)=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional nonlinear constraints, with LICQ and MFCQ used as representative local regularity conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A constraint-regularity failure at \(x\) is the failure of a declared constraint qualification. LICQ fails when \[\operatorname{rank} ig[
abla c_i(x)^T ig]_{i\in\mathcal E\cup\mathcal A_I(x)}<|\mathcal E|+|\mathcal A_I(x)|.\] MFCQ fails when either the equality gradients are linearly dependent or no \(w\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfies \[
abla c_i(x)^Tw=0\quad(i\in\mathcal E),\qquad 
abla c_i(x)^Tw>0\quad(i\in\mathcal A_I(x)).\] The qualification whose failure is asserted must be named because failure of LICQ does not imply failure of every weaker qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint-regularity failure occurs at a feasible point when a specified constraint qualification does not hold. LICQ failure means that the gradients of all equality constraints and active inequalities are linearly dependent. MFCQ failure means that the equality gradients are dependent or there is no direction tangent to every equality and strictly entering every active inequality. These are different boundaries: MFCQ can hold even when LICQ fails. Consequently, a record of regularity failure must identify the failed qualification rather than using an unqualified label.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Regularity failure is \(\neg\mathrm{CQ}(x)\) for an explicitly named constraint qualification \(\mathrm{CQ}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: LICQ fails exactly when there exists a nonzero coefficient vector on the active gradients whose linear combination is zero.
MFCQ failure is equivalent to the absence of the stated strict linearized feasible direction, together with possible dependence among equality gradients.
special_cases_latex: With only equalities, both displayed conditions reduce to full row rank of the equality Jacobian.
For linear active constraints, useful optimality conclusions may remain valid even if LICQ fails.
immediate_consequences_latex: LICQ failure can destroy uniqueness of KKT multipliers.
MFCQ failure removes the standard guarantee that the KKT multiplier set is bounded.
boundary_notes: Failure of a constraint qualification does not by itself imply that KKT multipliers do not exist.
Nonsmooth constraints require generalized derivatives and are outside this definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank deficiency of the active-constraint Jacobian
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(x\) be feasible and let \(A_{\mathrm{act}}(x)\in\mathbb R^{m_a\times n}\) have rows \(\nabla c_i(x)^T\) for all equality constraints and active inequalities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional constraints; the pathology concerns first-order active-gradient rank, not curvature of the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An active-constraint rank-deficiency pathology occurs at \(x\) when \[\operatorname{rank}A_{\mathrm{act}}(x)<m_a,\] equivalently, when there exists \(0
eq
u\in\mathbb R^{m_a}\) such that \[A_{\mathrm{act}}(x)^T
u=0.\] Its rank defect is \(\delta(x)=m_a-\operatorname{rank}A_{\mathrm{act}}(x)>0\). Thus LICQ fails, the standard active-set KKT matrix or Schur complement may be singular, and multiplier representations may be nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An active-constraint rank-deficiency pathology is present when the Jacobian formed from the equality constraints and active inequalities does not have full row rank. Equivalently, a nonzero linear combination of active gradients vanishes. The positive difference between the number of active rows and their rank measures the defect. This pathology violates LICQ and may make active-set linear systems singular or multiplier vectors nonunique. It does not necessarily change the feasible set, because redundant active constraints can cause rank deficiency while describing the same geometry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta(x)=m_a-\operatorname{rank}A_{\mathrm{act}}(x)>0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The smallest singular value associated with full row rank is zero.
There exists \(\nu\neq0\) in \(\ker A_{\mathrm{act}}(x)^T\).
special_cases_latex: If \(m_a>n\), rank deficiency is unavoidable.
Duplicate active constraints produce rank deficiency without necessarily altering the feasible region.
immediate_consequences_latex: The LICQ-based uniqueness conclusion for multipliers is unavailable.
A solver may replace the working set by an independent subset without deleting the redundant constraints from the mathematical problem.
boundary_notes: Rank deficiency does not imply MFCQ failure in every inequality-constrained problem.
Near rank deficiency with a small but nonzero singular value is ill conditioning, not exact rank deficiency.

knowledge_statements.title: Linearly Dependent Active Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of active-gradient independence and its effect on multiplier and working-set systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonlinear program with equalities \(h_j(x)=0\) and inequalities \(g_i(x)\leq0\), let \(I(x)=\{i:g_i(x)=0\}\). The active constraints are linearly dependent at a feasible point \(x\) when the family \(\{\nabla h_j(x)\}_j\cup\{\nabla g_i(x):i\in I(x)\}\) is linearly dependent. Equivalently, the active Jacobian has rank smaller than its number of rows. LICQ then fails. The associated KKT linear system may be singular and, when a multiplier exists, it need not be unique. Dependence is an algebraic failure boundary: removing redundant rows may restore a full-rank representation without changing the local feasible geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Active-gradient dependence violates LICQ, can make KKT systems singular and multipliers nonunique, yet may disappear after genuinely redundant constraints are removed.
assumptions_latex: The constraint functions are differentiable at the feasible point \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}J_{\mathrm{act}}(x)<\operatorname{rows}J_{\mathrm{act}}(x)\), so LICQ fails at \(x\).

notation.meaning: Jacobian of equality and active inequality constraints

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient Dependence Does Not Imply Local Redundancy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of algebraic active-gradient dependence from deletion invariance of the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \mathbb R^2 let g_1(x,y)=y-x^2 and g_2(x,y)=-y-x^2, with g_1\le0 and g_2\le0. At (0,0), both constraints are active and \nabla g_1(0,0)=(0,1), \nabla g_2(0,0)=(0,-1), so the active gradients are linearly dependent. Neither constraint is locally redundant: deleting g_1 admits points (0,y) with y>0, while deleting g_2 admits points (0,y) with y<0, none of which satisfy both original inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two opposite active gradients can be dependent even though each nonlinear inequality is locally essential.
assumptions_latex: Both inequalities use the nonpositive convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rank}J_{\mathrm{act}}(0,0)=1<2,\qquad g_1\text{ and }g_2\text{ are each locally nonredundant}.
knowledge_statements.title: Gradient Dependence Does Not Imply Local Redundancy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Network Bound-Activity Condition Ensuring Active-Constraint Independence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient condition for excluding the active-constraint rank-deficiency pathology in problem \((LP)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose that, at every network node, the bound constraints on \(\overline{dV}\) and \(\overline{dP}\) are not simultaneously active. Then the derivatives of the active equality and inequality constraints are linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the bounds on the two direction variables are never simultaneously active at a network node, the derivatives of all active equality and inequality constraints are linearly independent.
assumptions_latex: \text{At no network node are the bound constraints on }\overline{dV}\text{ and }\overline{dP}\text{ simultaneously active.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{Dg_i: i\text{ indexes an active equality or inequality constraint}\}\text{ is linearly independent.}

knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Active Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local redundancy of an active constraint in a nonlinear feasible-set representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{x:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), and let \(\bar x\in F\) satisfy \(g_r(\bar x)=0\). The active constraint indexed by \(r\) is locally redundant at \(\bar x\) if there exists a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that \[F\cap U=\{x\in U:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\leq0\ \text{for every}\ i\neq r\}.\] Thus deleting constraint \(r\) leaves the local feasible set unchanged. For example, in \(\mathbb{R}\), the constraints \(-x\leq0\) and \(-2x\leq0\) are both active at \(x=0\), and either one is redundant relative to the other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An active constraint is locally redundant when deleting it leaves the feasible set unchanged in some neighborhood of the point.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set is represented by equalities and inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Constraint \(r\) is locally redundant exactly when the displayed local feasible-set equality holds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Farkas Certificate for a Redundant Affine Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact global implication certificate for redundancy in a nonempty polyhedral system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let P_{-r}=\{x:A_{-r}x\ge b_{-r}\}\ne\varnothing. Inequality a_r^{\mathsf T}x\ge b_r is implied by P_{-r} if and only if there exists y\ge0 such that A_{-r}^{\mathsf T}y=a_r and b_{-r}^{\mathsf T}y\ge b_r. Thus y is an exact certificate that inequality r is globally redundant relative to the remaining affine system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative combination of the remaining affine inequalities certifies redundancy, and every implied affine inequality in a nonempty system has such a certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{-r}\subseteq\{x:a_r^{\mathsf T}x\ge b_r\}\iff\exists y\ge0:\ A_{-r}^{\mathsf T}y=a_r,\ b_{-r}^{\mathsf T}y\ge b_r.
knowledge_statements.title: Farkas Certificate for a Redundant Affine Inequality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization and local-geometry consequences of removing a locally redundant active constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If constraint r is locally redundant at \bar x, so that the original feasible set F and the set F_{-r} obtained by deleting r agree on a neighborhood U of \bar x, then \bar x is a local minimizer of f over F if and only if it is a local minimizer of f over F_{-r}. Their contingent tangent cones and their regular and limiting normal cones at \bar x also coincide. Multiplier representations need not coincide, because deleting r removes one coefficient from a possibly nonunique representation of a normal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting a locally redundant constraint preserves local minima and local tangent-normal geometry, although it can change multiplier representations.
assumptions_latex: F\cap U=F_{-r}\cap U for some neighborhood U of \bar x.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\in\operatorname{locmin}_F f\iff\bar x\in\operatorname{locmin}_{F_{-r}} f,\qquad T_F(\bar x)=T_{F_{-r}}(\bar x).

notation.meaning: feasible set after deleting constraint r

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Deficient Active Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank deficiency in a working-set representation of a polyhedral active face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\geq b\}\), let \(\bar x\in P\), and let \(I=\{i:a_i^{\mathsf T}\bar x=b_i\}\). The active-row representation at \(\bar x\) is rank deficient when \(\operatorname{rank}A_I<|I|\). The equality subspace used by a working-set step is \(E_I=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:A_Id=0\}=\ker A_I\). For any symmetric matrix \(H\), the full-row working-set KKT matrix \(K_I=\begin{pmatrix}H&A_I^{\mathsf T}\\A_I&0\end{pmatrix}\) is then singular: there exists \(y\neq0\) with \(A_I^{\mathsf T}y=0\), and hence \(K_I(0,y)^{\mathsf T}=0\). For \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}:x\geq0,\ 2x\geq0\}\) at \(\bar x=0\), the geometric active face is \(\{0\}\), while \(A_I=(1,2)^{\mathsf T}\) has one-dimensional rank and two rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral face can be geometrically well defined while its complete active-row representation is rank deficient. In that case the working-set equality subspace remains the kernel of the active matrix, but the KKT matrix retaining every dependent row is singular.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty polyhedron represented by \(Ax\geq b\).
\(I\) contains all inequalities active at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\operatorname{rank}A_I<|I|\), then the full-row working-set KKT matrix \(K_I\) is singular.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Independent-Row Representation of a Rank-Deficient Face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Row-basis repair preserving the face tangent and normal spaces while removing singularity caused solely by dependent multiplier rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A_I be the active-row matrix of a polyhedral face, and choose R\subseteq I so that the rows of A_R form a basis of \operatorname{row}(A_I). Then \ker A_R=\ker A_I and \operatorname{range}(A_R^{\mathsf T})=\operatorname{range}(A_I^{\mathsf T}), so the working-set equality directions and generated normal subspace are unchanged. If Z has columns forming a basis of \ker A_R, then the reduced-row KKT matrix K_R=\begin{pmatrix}H&A_R^{\mathsf T}\\A_R&0\end{pmatrix} is nonsingular if and only if Z^{\mathsf T}HZ is nonsingular. Thus row-basis extraction removes singularity caused by dependent multiplier rows but cannot repair singular reduced curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing all active rows by a row basis preserves the face tangent and normal spaces; the repaired KKT matrix is nonsingular exactly when the reduced Hessian is nonsingular.
assumptions_latex: The rows of A_R form a basis of the row space of A_I.
The columns of Z form a basis of \ker A_R.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ker A_R=\ker A_I,\quad \operatorname{range}(A_R^{\mathsf T})=\operatorname{range}(A_I^{\mathsf T}),\quad K_R\text{ nonsingular}\iff Z^{\mathsf T}HZ\text{ nonsingular}.

notation.meaning: indices of a maximal independent active-row subset
basis matrix for the working-set null space
KKT matrix formed from the independent active rows

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Minimum With Only Abnormal Fritz John Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar example where failed regularity destroys KKT necessity while abnormal Fritz John stationarity remains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Minimize f(x)=x subject to g(x)=x^2\le0. The feasible set is \{0\}, so \bar x=0 is a local and global minimizer. Since f'(0)=1 and g'(0)=0, no \lambda\ge0 satisfies f'(0)+\lambda g'(0)=0; hence KKT stationarity fails. Nevertheless, the nonzero Fritz John tuple (\mu_0,\lambda)=(0,1) satisfies \mu_0f'(0)+\lambda g'(0)=0 and \lambda g(0)=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The singleton constraint x²≤0 makes zero optimal, but its vanishing gradient prevents KKT stationarity and leaves an abnormal Fritz John tuple.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x=0\text{ is optimal},\quad \nexists\lambda\ge0:\ 1+\lambda\,0=0,\quad (\mu_0,\lambda)=(0,1)\text{ is Fritz John}.

notation.meaning: objective coefficient in Fritz John stationarity

knowledge_statements.title: Local Minimum With Only Abnormal Fritz John Information

knowledge_statements.statement_title: MFCQ Excludes Exactly the Abnormal Multiplier System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternative characterization connecting abnormal multipliers with failure of the Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a feasible point  ar x of h(x)=0 and g(x)\le0, MFCQ holds if and only if the only pair (
u,\lambda) satisfying J_h( ar x)^{\mathsf T}
u+J_g( ar x)^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0, \lambda\ge0, and \lambda_i g_i( ar x)=0 is (
u,\lambda)=(0,0). Consequently, every nonzero Fritz John multiplier tuple at a local minimizer under MFCQ has a positive objective coefficient and can be normalized to a KKT multiplier tuple.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MFCQ is equivalent to exclusion of nonzero abnormal constraint multipliers, so Fritz John multipliers normalize to KKT multipliers under MFCQ.
assumptions_latex: h and g are differentiable at the feasible point \bar x.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{MFCQ}(\bar x)\Longrightarrow \mu_0>0\text{ for every nonzero Fritz John tuple }(\mu_0,\nu,\lambda).
knowledge_statements.title: MFCQ Excludes Exactly the Abnormal Multiplier System
Abnormal-Multiplier Pathologies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fritz John stationarity with a zero objective multiplier under failed constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For minimizing \(f(x)\) subject to \(h(x)=0\) and \(g(x)\leq0\), a feasible point \( ar x\) has an abnormal-multiplier pathology if there exist \((
u,\lambda)
eq(0,0)\), with \(\lambda_i\geq0\) and \(\lambda_i g_i( ar x)=0\), such that \[J_h( ar x)^{\mathsf T}
u+J_g( ar x)^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0.\] These are Fritz John multipliers with objective multiplier equal to zero. Their existence means the stationarity relation can be supported entirely by constraint normals, so normalization to an objective multiplier of one is unavailable from this multiplier tuple. Standard constraint qualifications exclude such nonzero abnormal multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An abnormal multiplier is a nonzero signed combination of active constraint gradients that vanishes without involving the objective gradient, obstructing Fritz John normalization.
assumptions_latex: \(f\), \(h\), and \(g\) are differentiable at the feasible point \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonzero \((\nu,\lambda)\) satisfying the displayed homogeneous constraint-stationarity system is an abnormal multiplier.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Abnormal Fritz John multiplier at a feasible point
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(h_i(x)=0\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and \(g_j(x)\leq0\), \(j=1,\ldots,r\), with continuously differentiable data. Let \(\mathcal A(x)=\{j:g_j(x)=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order finite-dimensional smooth nonlinear programming, using the Fritz John objective multiplier to distinguish normal and abnormal systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An abnormal multiplier system at a feasible point \(x\) is a nonzero pair \((\lambda,\mu)\), with \(\mu_j\geq0\) and \(\mu_jg_j(x)=0\), satisfying \[\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i
abla h_i(x)+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j
abla g_j(x)=0.\] Equivalently, it is a Fritz John multiplier triple \((\mu_0,\lambda,\mu)
eq0\) satisfying stationarity with objective multiplier \(\mu_0=0\). A feasible point is abnormal when at least one such system exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An abnormal-multiplier pathology occurs when the Fritz John stationarity conditions can be satisfied with zero coefficient on the objective gradient and nonzero constraint multipliers. Equality multipliers are unrestricted, inequality multipliers are nonnegative, and complementary slackness restricts nonzero inequality multipliers to active constraints. Because the objective disappears from the stationarity equation, the multiplier system reflects degeneracy of the constraint description rather than ordinary KKT balance. A constraint qualification that excludes all nonzero abnormal systems permits normalization of the objective multiplier to one and recovery of KKT multipliers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Abnormality is the existence of \((\lambda,\mu)\neq0\) satisfying constraint-only stationarity, inequality nonnegativity, and complementarity.
equivalent_formulations_latex: There is a Fritz John multiplier with \(\mu_0=0\).
The active constraint gradients admit a nontrivial signed-conic dependence compatible with the inequality multiplier signs.
special_cases_latex: With equality constraints only, abnormality is equivalent to linear dependence of their gradients.
Under MFCQ, an abnormal Fritz John system is excluded.
immediate_consequences_latex: The Fritz John system cannot necessarily be normalized to a KKT system.
The existence of an abnormal system does not preclude the simultaneous existence of a normal multiplier system.
boundary_notes: A zero KKT multiplier on one weakly active constraint is not by itself an abnormal Fritz John system.
Sign conventions change if inequalities are written as \(g_j(x)\geq0\).

notation.meaning: Fritz John multiplier on the objective gradient.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spurious Linearized Descent at a Constrained Minimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization consequence of the cusp tangent-versus-linearization mismatch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let F=\{(x_1,x_2):x_2^2-x_1^3\le0\} and minimize f(x_1,x_2)=x_1 over F. Every feasible point has x_1\ge0, so  ar x=(0,0) is a global minimizer. The constraint gradient vanishes at  ar x, hence L_F( ar x)=\mathbb R^2, and d=(-1,0) is a linearized feasible direction with 
abla f( ar x)^{\mathsf T}d=-1. But T_F( ar x)=\{(d_1,0):d_1\ge0\}, so d is not a true tangent direction. Moreover, no inequality multiplier satisfies 
abla f( ar x)+\lambda
abla g( ar x)=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the cusp minimum, linearization falsely admits a descent direction that no feasible curve can follow, and ordinary KKT stationarity fails.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
ar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{F}f,\qquad (-1,0)\in L_F( ar x)\setminus T_F( ar x),\qquad 
exists\lambda\ge0:\ 
abla f( ar x)+\lambda
abla g( ar x)=0.
knowledge_statements.title: Spurious Linearized Descent at a Constrained Minimum
Linearization–Geometry Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict enlargement of the tangent cone by first-order linearized constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F=\{x:h(x)=0,\ g(x)\leq0\}\), define the linearized cone at \(\bar x\in F\) by \(L_F(\bar x)=\{d:J_h(\bar x)d=0,\ \nabla g_i(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}d\leq0\text{ for }i\in I(\bar x)\}\). Always \(T_F(\bar x)\subseteq L_F(\bar x)\); a linearization–geometry mismatch occurs when inclusion is strict. For \(F=\{(x_1,x_2):x_2^2-x_1^3\leq0\}\) at the origin, the constraint gradient vanishes, so \(L_F(0)=\mathbb{R}^2\), whereas \(T_F(0)=\{(d_1,0):d_1\geq0\}\). Thus first-order linearization admits directions absent from the true feasible geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without suitable regularity, the linearized cone can strictly exceed the tangent cone; a cusp with vanishing constraint gradient exhibits the mismatch explicitly.
assumptions_latex: The constraints are differentiable at \(\bar x\).
\(T_F(\bar x)\) is the contingent tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For the cusp example, \(T_F(0)\subsetneq L_F(0)=\mathbb{R}^2\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mismatch between the linearized cone and tangent geometry
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Omega=\{x:c_i(x)=0\ (i\in\mathcal E),\ c_i(x)\geq0\ (i\in\mathcal I)\}\), and let \(x\in\Omega\). Denote the tangent cone by \(T_\Omega(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order local geometry of a smooth finite-dimensional feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linearized feasible-direction cone at \(x\) is \[F(x)=\{d:\nabla c_i(x)^Td=0\ (i\in\mathcal E),\ \nabla c_i(x)^Td\geq0\ (i\in\mathcal A_I(x))\}.\] A linearization–geometry mismatch occurs when \[T_\Omega(x)\subsetneq F(x).\] Equivalently, there exists \(d\in F(x)\) that is not realizable as a tangent direction of feasible points approaching \(x\). The mismatch is exact when the inclusion is strict; equality \(T_\Omega(x)=F(x)\) means that first-order linearization captures the tangent geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The linearized cone contains directions satisfying the first-order equality equations and active-inequality inequalities. The tangent cone contains limits of actual feasible secant directions. A linearization–geometry mismatch occurs when the linearized cone is strictly larger: it predicts at least one first-order feasible direction that cannot arise from nearby feasible points. This is the geometric pathology that constraint qualifications are designed to exclude. It can be extreme, for example when the feasible set is locally a single point but the vanishing constraint gradients make the linearized cone contain nonzero directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Mismatch is the strict inclusion \(T_\Omega(x)\subsetneq F(x)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exists \(d\) satisfying all linearized active constraints such that no feasible sequences \(x_j\to x\) and \(t_j\downarrow0\) satisfy \((x_j-x)/t_j\to d\).
special_cases_latex: Under LICQ for smooth constraints, the cited tangent-cone result gives \(T_\Omega(x)=F(x)\), so this mismatch is absent.
If \(\Omega=\{x\}\) locally but \(F(x)\neq\{0\}\), the mismatch is immediate.
immediate_consequences_latex: A descent direction in \(F(x)\setminus T_\Omega(x)\) does not certify the existence of a nearby feasible descent path.
KKT arguments based only on the linearized cone require an appropriate qualification when mismatch is possible.
boundary_notes: The reverse strict inclusion is not the standard smooth-constraint relation; tangent directions satisfy the linearized constraints under the stated differentiability assumptions.
Equality of the cones can hold even when a commonly used sufficient constraint qualification fails.

notation.meaning: Tangent cone of the feasible set at x.
Cone of first-order feasible directions defined by active-constraint linearization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual-Complementarity Degeneracy at a KKT Point
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider c(\min_x f(x)\) subject to c(h(x)=0\) and c(g(x)\le 0\), where the data are continuously differentiable. At a feasible point c(\bar x\), let c(A(\bar x)=\{i:g_i(\bar x)=0\}\), c(L(x,\lambda,\mu)=f(x)+\lambda^Th(x)+\mu^Tg(x)\), and let c(\Lambda(\bar x)\) be the set of KKT multipliers satisfying stationarity, c(\mu\ge0\), and complementarity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth nonlinear programming; the definition is an umbrella classification for degeneracy in the dual variables or complementarity pattern at a KKT point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A KKT point c(\bar x\) is dual-complementarity degenerate if its nonempty multiplier set c(\Lambda(\bar x)\) has at least one of the following properties: c(\Lambda(\bar x)\) is unbounded; c(\Lambda(\bar x)\) is not a singleton; no multiplier is strictly complementary, meaning c(\forall(\lambda,\mu)\in\Lambda(\bar x)\;\exists i\in A(\bar x):\mu_i=0\); or the positive-multiplier active set c(A^+(\mu)=\{i\in A(\bar x):\mu_i>0\}\) depends on the selected multiplier. The last property means that there exist c((\lambda^1,\mu^1),(\lambda^2,\mu^2)\in\Lambda(\bar x)\) and c(i\in A(\bar x)\) with c(\mu_i^1>0\) and c(\mu_i^2=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth NLP KKT point is dual-complementarity degenerate when its KKT multiplier set is unbounded or nonunique, when every admissible multiplier has a zero component on some active inequality, or when different multipliers classify an active inequality differently as strongly or weakly active.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c(\bar x\text{ is dual-complementarity degenerate}\iff \Lambda(\bar x)\text{ satisfies at least one listed dual or complementarity pathology}.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Failure of strict complementarity is c(\nexists(\lambda,\mu)\in\Lambda(\bar x)\) such that c(\mu_i>0\) for every c(i\in A(\bar x)\).
Multiplier-dependent activity is equivalently c(A^+(\mu^1)\ne A^+(\mu^2)\) for some two KKT multipliers.
special_cases_latex: Under LICQ, the multiplier is unique; hence only strict-complementarity failure remains among the listed pathologies.
Under MFCQ, a nonempty KKT multiplier set is bounded, so unbounded-multiplier degeneracy is excluded.
immediate_consequences_latex: The active set c(A(\bar x)\) need not determine a unique positive-multiplier subset.
A zero multiplier on an active inequality leaves complementarity unable to distinguish that constraint from one about to become inactive.
boundary_notes: This definition does not classify primal constraint-qualification failure unless it manifests through the multiplier set.
Equality multipliers are unrestricted in sign; strict complementarity concerns inequality multipliers only.

notation.meaning: Set of all KKT multiplier pairs at the feasible point.
Active inequalities having strictly positive multiplier under c(\mu\).

knowledge_statements.title: Zero Active Multipliers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weakly active inequalities whose KKT multipliers vanish, causing strict-complementarity failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a KKT point \(x_*\) for inequalities \(g_i(x)\leq0\), an active index \(i\) has a zero active multiplier when \(g_i(x_*)=0\) and \(\lambda_i^*=0\). Such an index is weakly active and violates strict complementarity, which would require \(\lambda_i^*>0\) for every active inequality. For the problem \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}}x^2\) subject to \(-x\leq0\), the unique solution is \(x_*=0\), the constraint is active, and stationarity gives \(2x_* -\lambda^*=0\), hence \(\lambda^*=0\). Therefore optimality can hold while multiplier signs provide no strict margin for stable active-set identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero multiplier on an active inequality violates strict complementarity; optimality may remain valid, but multiplier-based active-set identification loses its strict sign margin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_i(x_*)=0\) and \(\lambda_i^*=0\) imply failure of strict complementarity at index \(i\).

notation.meaning: KKT multiplier of inequality index i

knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Multiplier Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes KKT multiplier nonuniqueness at a fixed feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider minimizing \(f(x)\) subject to \(h(x)=0\) and \(g(x)\le 0\), with continuously differentiable data. For a feasible point \(x^*\), let \(I(x^*)=\{i:g_i(x^*)=0\}\) and define
\[\mathcal M(x^*)=\{(
u,\lambda):
abla f(x^*)+
abla h(x^*)^T
u+
abla g(x^*)^T\lambda=0,\ \lambda\ge0,\ \lambda_i g_i(x^*)=0\}.\]
The multiplier set is nonunique exactly when there exist distinct \((
u^1,\lambda^1),(
u^2,\lambda^2)\in\mathcal M(x^*)\). Equivalently, their nonzero difference lies in the nullspace of the active-constraint gradient matrix while both endpoints satisfy the multiplier sign restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: KKT multipliers are nonunique when two distinct sign-feasible multiplier vectors satisfy stationarity and complementarity at the same feasible point.

notation.meaning: active inequality index set at the fixed point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates multiplier nonuniqueness from the stronger sibling pathology of unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R}x\) subject to \(g_1(x)=-x\le0\) and \(g_2(x)=-2x\le0\). The global minimizer is \(x^*=0\), and \(\mathcal M(0)=\{(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)\in\mathbb R_+^2:1-\lambda_1-2\lambda_2=0\}\), a nontrivial compact line segment. Thus KKT multipliers can be nonunique without being unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two redundant active inequalities produce a compact segment of KKT multipliers, proving that nonuniqueness does not imply unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\mathcal M(0)|>1\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal M(0)\text{ is bounded}.

notation.meaning: KKT multiplier set at the solution zero

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiplier Set as a Convex Polyhedron
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural representation of all KKT multipliers at one fixed feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a fixed feasible point \(x^*\), the KKT multiplier set \(\mathcal M(x^*)\) is the intersection of an affine stationarity space with \(\lambda_i=0\) for inactive inequalities and \(\lambda_i\ge0\) for active inequalities. Hence \(\mathcal M(x^*)\) is a closed convex polyhedron. If \(m^1,m^2\in\mathcal M(x^*)\), then \((1-t)m^1+tm^2\in\mathcal M(x^*)\) for every \(t\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The multiplier set at a fixed feasible point is a closed convex polyhedron, so two distinct multipliers generate an entire multiplier segment.
assumptions_latex: The objective and constraints are continuously differentiable at the feasible point \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal M(x^*)\text{ is a closed convex polyhedron.}

notation.meaning: KKT multiplier set at the fixed feasible point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies recession directions that make the KKT multiplier set at a fixed feasible point unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R\), \(h:\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R^p\), and \(g:\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable, and consider minimizing \(f(x)\) subject to \(h(x)=0\) and \(g(x)\le 0\). For a feasible point \(x^*\), define \(I(x^*)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:g_i(x^*)=0\}\) and
\[\mathcal M(x^*)=\{(
u,\lambda)\in\mathbb R^p	imes\mathbb R^m:
abla f(x^*)+
abla h(x^*)^T
u+
abla g(x^*)^T\lambda=0,\ \lambda_i\ge0\ (i\in I(x^*)),\ \lambda_i=0\ (i
otin I(x^*))\}.\]
If \(\mathcal M(x^*)
eq\varnothing\), then it is unbounded if and only if there is a nonzero pair \((u,v)\in\mathbb R^p	imes\mathbb R^m\) satisfying
\[
abla h(x^*)^Tu+
abla g(x^*)^Tv=0,\qquad v_i\ge0\ (i\in I(x^*)),\qquad v_i=0\ (i
otin I(x^*)).\]
In that case, for every \((
u,\lambda)\in\mathcal M(x^*)\) and every \(t\ge0\), one has \((
u+tu,\lambda+tv)\in\mathcal M(x^*)\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For the smooth NLP c(\min f(x)\) subject to c(h(x)=0\) and c(g(x)\le0\), define c(L=f+\lambda^Th+\mu^Tg\). At a feasible point c(\bar x\), set c(\Lambda(\bar x)=\{(\lambda,\mu):\nabla_xL(\bar x,\lambda,\mu)=0,\ \mu\ge0,\ \mu_i g_i(\bar x)=0\ \forall i\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth NLP with Euclidean norms; the definition concerns exact KKT multipliers at one fixed feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The KKT multiplier set at c(\bar x\) is unbounded if it is nonempty and c(\sup\{\|(\lambda,\mu)\|:(\lambda,\mu)\in\Lambda(\bar x)\}=+\infty\). Equivalently, for every c(M>0\) there exists c((\lambda_M,\mu_M)\in\Lambda(\bar x)\) with c(\|(\lambda_M,\mu_M)\|>M\). Thus the same primal stationary point admits exact dual certificates of arbitrarily large norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point has an unbounded multiplier set when it has at least one KKT multiplier and, for every finite bound, it has another KKT multiplier whose norm exceeds that bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c(\Lambda(\bar x)\ne\varnothing\quad\text{and}\quad\sup_{(\lambda,\mu)\in\Lambda(\bar x)}\|(\lambda,\mu)\|=+\infty.
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exists a sequence c((\lambda^k,\mu^k)\in\Lambda(\bar x)\) such that c(\|(\lambda^k,\mu^k)\|\to\infty\).
Because all norms are equivalent in finite dimensions, unboundedness does not depend on the chosen vector norm.
special_cases_latex: MFCQ, or Robinson regularity in the set-constrained formulation, implies boundedness of a nonempty multiplier set and therefore excludes this case.
LICQ makes the KKT multiplier unique whenever it exists, hence bounded.
immediate_consequences_latex: No finite uniform bound can be imposed on exact dual certificates at c(\bar x\).
Normalized unbounded sequences may expose a nonzero abnormal multiplier satisfying the homogeneous stationarity and sign relations.
boundary_notes: An empty multiplier set is not called unbounded here; it is a failure of multiplier existence.
Large but finite multiplier norms are conditioning concerns, not mathematical unboundedness.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Complementarity Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the convention \(g_i(x)\le0\) and \(\lambda_i\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((x^*,\nu^*,\lambda^*)\) satisfy the KKT conditions for minimizing \(f(x)\) subject to \(h(x)=0\) and \(g(x)\le0\). Strict complementarity holds at this KKT triple when
\[g_i(x^*)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\lambda_i^*>0\]
for every inequality index \(i\). It fails at the triple precisely when some active inequality has zero multiplier:
\[\exists i\in I(x^*)\quad \lambda_i^*=0.\]
Strict complementarity fails intrinsically at \(x^*\) when every multiplier pair in \(\mathcal M(x^*)\) has at least one zero component indexed by \(I(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict complementarity fails when an active inequality has zero multiplier; intrinsic failure means no KKT multiplier is positive on every active inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists i\in I(x^*):\lambda_i^*=0\).

notation.meaning: KKT multiplier set at the point

children.title: Multiplier-Sign Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Cases where degeneracy obscures stable sign-based interpretation of active multipliers.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sign-Ambiguous Stationarity with a Unique KKT Multiplier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates unrestricted stationary sign ambiguity from KKT multiplier nonuniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{(x_1,x_2)}-x_1\) subject to \(g_1(x)=x_1\le0\), \(g_2(x)=x_2\le0\), and \(g_3(x)=x_2\le0\), at \(x^*=(0,0)\). The unrestricted stationary multiplier set is \(\mathcal S(x^*)=\{(1,t,-t):t\in\mathbb R\}\). Components two and three attain both signs, but imposing \(\lambda\ge0\) forces \(t=0\). Hence the KKT multiplier set is the singleton \(\{(1,0,0)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Redundant active constraints can make unrestricted stationary components change sign even though the sign-feasible KKT multiplier is unique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal S(x^*)=\{(1,t,-t):t\in\mathbb R\},\qquad \mathcal M(x^*)=\{(1,0,0)\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Sign-Ambiguous Stationarity with a Unique KKT Multiplier

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes sign variation in the unrestricted stationarity solution set from multiplicity of sign-feasible KKT multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible point \(x^*\), let \(\mathcal S(x^*)\) be the affine set of multiplier pairs satisfying stationarity and zero multipliers on inactive inequalities, without imposing signs on active inequality multipliers. An active index \(j\) has stationary-multiplier sign ambiguity when there exist \(m^+,m^-\in\mathcal S(x^*)\) with \(\lambda_j^+>0>\lambda_j^-\). Under \(g\le0\), only members of \(\mathcal S(x^*)\) having \(\lambda\ge0\) are KKT multipliers. Thus sign ambiguity in \(\mathcal S(x^*)\) neither asserts two KKT multipliers nor makes a negative component dual feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sign ambiguity means the unrestricted stationary multiplier equations allow opposite signs for an active component, although only nonnegative solutions are KKT multipliers.
assumptions_latex: The objective and constraints are continuously differentiable at the feasible point \(x^*\).
Inequalities use \(g(x)\le0\) and KKT multipliers use \(\lambda\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists j\in I(x^*),\ m^+,m^-\in\mathcal S(x^*):\lambda_j^+>0>\lambda_j^-.

notation.meaning: stationarity solution set before inequality-multiplier sign restrictions
multiplier component for active inequality j

knowledge_statements.title: Unrestricted Stationary Multiplier Sign Ambiguity
Multiplier-Sign Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes stationary multiplier solutions from sign-feasible KKT multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a feasible point \(x^*\), define the stationary multiplier set without inequality signs by
\[\mathcal S(x^*)=\{(
u,\lambda):
abla f(x^*)+
abla h(x^*)^T
u+
abla g(x^*)^T\lambda=0,\ \lambda_i=0\ 	ext{if}\ i
otin I(x^*)\}.\]
Multiplier-sign ambiguity occurs for an active index \(j\) when \(\mathcal S(x^*)\) contains two pairs whose \(j\)-components have opposite signs. Under the convention \(g\le0\), only elements with \(\lambda\ge0\) are KKT multipliers; hence a negative stationary component is not itself a valid KKT multiplier but exposes degeneracy or unreliable sign-based active-set classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sign ambiguity occurs when stationary multiplier equations permit opposite signs for one active constraint, although only nonnegative values satisfy KKT dual feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(f,h,g\) are continuously differentiable at the feasible point \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists j\in I(x^*),\ (\nu^+,\lambda^+),(\nu^-,\lambda^-)\in\mathcal S(x^*):\lambda_j^+>0>\lambda_j^-\).

notation.meaning: stationary multiplier set before dual sign restrictions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Curvature Degeneracy on the Critical Cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let c(\bar x\) be a KKT point of a twice continuously differentiable NLP, let c((\bar\lambda,\bar\mu)\) be a KKT multiplier, let c(C(\bar x,\bar\lambda,\bar\mu)\) be its critical cone, and write c(H=\nabla_{xx}^2L(\bar x,\bar\lambda,\bar\mu)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth NLP at a specified KKT primal-dual pair; curvature is tested only in first-order critical directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the critical curvature modulus c(\gamma(\bar x,\bar\lambda,\bar\mu)=\inf\{d^THd:d\in C(\bar x,\bar\lambda,\bar\mu),\ \|d\|=1\}\), with c(\gamma=+\infty\) when the critical cone contains no unit vector. The KKT pair is curvature degenerate when c(\gamma\le0\), equivalently when there is no constant c(\sigma>0\) satisfying c(d^THd\ge\sigma\|d\|^2\) for every critical direction c(d\). Exact curvature degeneracy has c(\gamma=0\); negative-curvature failure has c(\gamma<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A KKT pair is curvature degenerate when the Lagrangian Hessian lacks a uniform positive lower bound on the critical cone. Zero minimum curvature is exact degeneracy, while negative minimum curvature is a stronger second-order failure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c(\gamma(\bar x,\bar\lambda,\bar\mu)\le0\iff \nexists\sigma>0\ \forall d\in C:\ d^T\nabla_{xx}^2L\,d\ge\sigma\|d\|^2.
equivalent_formulations_latex: In finite dimensions, c(\gamma>0\) is equivalent to strict positivity c(d^THd>0\) for every nonzero c(d\in C\).
When c(C\) is a linear subspace with basis matrix c(Z\), degeneracy is equivalent to c(\lambda_{\min}(Z^THZ)\le0\) after choosing orthonormal columns.
special_cases_latex: For an unconstrained stationary point, c(C=\mathbb R^n\), so curvature degeneracy is c(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(\bar x))\le0\).
Under unique multipliers and strict complementarity, the critical cone is the null space of the active-constraint Jacobian.
immediate_consequences_latex: The standard second-order sufficient condition at the specified multiplier fails.
If c(\gamma=0\), arbitrarily flat unit critical directions exist; in finite dimensions the infimum is attained.
boundary_notes: The definition is multiplier-relative when KKT multipliers are nonunique.
Positive semidefiniteness with a zero critical eigenvalue is distinct from negative curvature.

notation.meaning: Critical cone for the specified KKT pair.

knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Reduced Curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of positive-definite Lagrangian curvature on the critical cone of a specified KKT triple.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((x^*,\nu^*,\lambda^*)\) be a KKT triple for a twice continuously differentiable nonlinear program. Let \(C(x^*,\lambda^*)\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) denote the critical cone associated with this triple, and define
\[H=\nabla_{xx}^2L(x^*,\nu^*,\lambda^*).\]
Strict reduced curvature holds for this triple when
\[d^THd>0\qquad\text{for every }d\in C(x^*,\lambda^*)\setminus\{0\}.\]
Loss of reduced curvature occurs precisely when
\[\exists d\in C(x^*,\lambda^*)\setminus\{0\}:d^THd\le0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced curvature is lost for a specified KKT triple when the Lagrangian Hessian is nonpositive along a nonzero direction in its critical cone.
assumptions_latex: The objective and constraints are twice continuously differentiable near \(x^*\).
\(C(x^*,\lambda^*)\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the critical cone associated with the specified KKT triple.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists d\in C(x^*,\lambda^*)\setminus\{0\}:d^T\nabla_{xx}^2L(x^*,\nu^*,\lambda^*)d\le0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Flat Curvature Does Not Preclude a Strict Minimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary example showing that loss through zero curvature does not imply nonoptimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R}x^4\), the point \(x^*=0\) is the unique global minimizer, but \(\nabla^2f(0)=0\). The critical cone is \(\mathbb R\), and \(d^T\nabla^2f(0)d=0\) for every nonzero \(d\). Thus strict reduced curvature is lost although strict local and global optimality hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strict minimizer of x to the fourth has zero Hessian, so loss of strict reduced curvature alone does not disprove optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*=0\text{ is a strict global minimizer and }d^T\nabla^2f(0)d=0\text{ for every }d\ne0.
knowledge_statements.title: Flat Curvature Does Not Preclude a Strict Minimum

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes inconclusive loss of strict curvature from violation of reduced positive semidefiniteness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\nabla_{xx}^2L(x^*,\nu^*,\lambda^*)\) and let \(C\) be the critical cone of the specified KKT triple. Loss of strict reduced curvature has two cases: \(d^THd=0\) for some nonzero \(d\in C\), or \(d^THd<0\) for some nonzero \(d\in C\). The zero-curvature case defeats strict positive-curvature sufficiency but is compatible with local optimality. The negative-curvature case additionally violates any applicable second-order necessary condition requiring \(d^THd\ge0\) on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero reduced curvature makes the strict second-order test inconclusive, whereas negative reduced curvature violates applicable reduced positive-semidefiniteness conditions.
assumptions_latex: The problem data are twice continuously differentiable near \(x^*\).
\(C\) is the critical cone used by the applicable second-order condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\exists d\in C\setminus\{0\}:d^THd=0\bigr)\ \text{is inconclusive, whereas}\ \bigl(\exists d\in C\setminus\{0\}:d^THd<0\bigr)\ \text{violates reduced positive semidefiniteness}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of Positive Curvature in the Reduced Hessian
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: At a smooth NLP KKT pair c((\bar x,\bar\lambda,\bar\mu)\), suppose the active-constraint Jacobian c(A\) has full row rank and strict complementarity holds. Let c(Z\) have orthonormal columns spanning c(\ker A\), let c(H=\nabla_{xx}^2L(\bar x,\bar\lambda,\bar\mu)\), and define the reduced Hessian c(R=Z^THZ\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional NLP in the regime where the critical cone reduces to the active-manifold tangent subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Reduced curvature is lost at the KKT pair when c(R\) is not positive definite, equivalently c(\lambda_{\min}(R)\le0\). Thus there exists a nonzero reduced coordinate c(u\) such that c(u^TRu\le0\), or equivalently a nonzero tangent direction c(d=Zu\in\ker A\) with c(d^THd\le0\). The boundary case c(\lambda_{\min}(R)=0\) is singular reduced curvature; a negative eigenvalue is an indefinite reduced-curvature failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Loss of reduced curvature means that the Lagrangian Hessian, after restriction to directions tangent to all active constraints, is not positive definite. It therefore has a zero or negative curvature direction in the null space of the active Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c(R=Z^THZ\not\succ0\iff \exists u\ne0:\ u^TRu\le0\iff\exists d\in\ker A\setminus\{0\}:d^THd\le0.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For orthonormal c(Z\), loss occurs exactly when c(\lambda_{\min}(Z^THZ)\le0\).
The property is independent of the chosen basis: if c(\widetilde Z=ZT\) with nonsingular c(T\), then c(\widetilde Z^TH\widetilde Z\succ0\iff Z^THZ\succ0\).
special_cases_latex: If c(\ker A=\{0\}\), there are no nonzero reduced directions, so reduced curvature is vacuously positive.
For equality-constrained quadratic programming, c(H\) is the objective Hessian and c(R\) is the standard reduced Hessian.
immediate_consequences_latex: The reduced-Hessian form of the second-order sufficient condition fails.
A singular reduced Hessian also destroys the standard nonsingularity guarantee for the associated KKT matrix.
boundary_notes: Without strict complementarity, the critical cone need not equal c(\ker A\); a critical-cone test is then the more faithful condition.
Ill-conditioning with a small positive eigenvalue is near-loss, not exact loss.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: All-Active-Equalities Test Misses Weak-Activity Negative Curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional realization of the weak-activity curvature-omission criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R}-x^2\) subject to \(g(x)=-x\le0\). At \(x^*=0\), stationarity holds with the active multiplier \(\lambda^*=0\). The critical cone is \(C=\{d:d\ge0\}\), whereas treating the active inequality as an equality gives \(T_A=\{0\}\). For every \(d>0\), \(d^T\nabla_{xx}^2L(0,0)d=-2d^2<0\). Thus the equality-space test is vacuous while the correct critical-cone test detects negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly active inequality permits inward negative-curvature directions that disappear when all active inequalities are imposed as equalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_A=\{0\}\subsetneq C=\mathbb R_+\quad\text{and}\quad d^T\nabla_{xx}^2L(0,0)d<0\ \forall d\in C\setminus\{0\}.

notation.meaning: critical cone at the KKT pair

knowledge_statements.title: All-Active-Equalities Test Misses Weak-Activity Negative Curvature

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General criterion for a false curvature conclusion caused by treating weakly active inequalities as equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a KKT triple, let \(I_+=\{i:\lambda_i^*>0\}\), \(I_0=\{i:\lambda_i^*=0\}\), let \(C\) be the critical cone, and define the all-active-equalities space \(T_A=\{d:
abla h(x^*)d=0,\ 
abla g_i(x^*)d=0\ (i\in I_+\cup I_0)\}\). Then \(T_A\subseteq C\). A weak-activity curvature omission occurs when \(d^THd\ge0\) for every \(d\in T_A\), but some \(d\in C\setminus T_A\) satisfies \(d^THd<0\), where \(H=
abla_{xx}^2L(x^*,
u^*,\lambda^*)\). The omitted direction must be strictly inward for at least one weakly active inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treating every active inequality as an equality can omit weakly inward critical directions and thereby miss negative Lagrangian curvature.
assumptions_latex: The problem data are twice continuously differentiable near \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\forall d\in T_A,\ d^THd\ge0\bigr]\ \land\ \bigl[\exists d\in C\setminus T_A:\ d^THd<0\bigr].

knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Activity Curvature Omission Criterion
Weak-Activity Curvature Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows how zero active multipliers alter the direction set used for curvature tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a KKT triple, partition the active inequalities into \(I_+=\{i:\lambda_i^*>0\}\) and \(I_0=\{i:\lambda_i^*=0\}\). The multiplier-dependent critical cone is
\[C=\{d:
abla h(x^*)d=0,\ 
abla g_i(x^*)d=0\ (i\in I_+),\ 
abla g_i(x^*)d\le0\ (i\in I_0),\ 
abla f(x^*)^Td=0\}.\]
Weak-activity curvature ambiguity is present when some \(d\in C\) has \(
abla g_j(x^*)d<0\) for a weakly active \(j\in I_0\). Such a direction is retained by the critical-cone test but would be excluded if every active constraint were incorrectly imposed as a linearized equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-multiplier active constraint permits inward critical directions that an all-active-equalities curvature test would wrongly exclude.
assumptions_latex: The objective and constraints are twice continuously differentiable near \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists j\in I_0,\ d\in C:\nabla g_j(x^*)d<0\).
